The reported case was `from System.User`, but it is **not System-specific** — `from Administration.Account` fails identically, and a guard keyed on System would pass the general case through; the rule is the module boundary. Control both ways: the supported direction (`from MyModule.X to System.User`) and a plain same-module association must stay at 0 errors, and stubbing the guard must bring the KeyNotFoundException back. To locate a dangling GUID at all, scan every `.mxunit` for the raw 16 bytes in BOTH endiannesses (`uuid.bytes` and `uuid.bytes_le` — little-endian is the one that hits). **Run `make check-mdl` before pushing any new `mdl-examples/` file**: CI runs every example as a POSITIVE test unless it is named `*.fail.mdl`, so a fixture demonstrating a refusal fails the build. Split it — refused statements in the `.fail.mdl`, working forms in a sibling `.mdl`, each pointing at the other — so both halves are actually gated rather than only the negative one. ako/mxcli-captrack |
| A test fails only on CI and never locally — e.g. `TestWatcherDebounce`: `expected 1 debounced message, got 2` | The test ASSUMED a timing premise instead of checking it. A debounce test needs the whole burst of writes to land inside the debounce window; each write resets the timer, so a gap larger than the window splits the burst and it debounces as two. On a loaded runner one gap between five `os.WriteFile` calls exceeded 500ms | `cmd/mxcli/tui/watcher.go` (`newWatcherDebounced`, the window is a field not a constant), `cmd/mxcli/tui/watcher_test.go` | **Get the observed value out of the CI log before theorising** — `gh run view <id> --log \| grep <test>`. I guessed "count 0, event delivery too slow" and built two controls for it; both passed, because the log said `got 2` and the real mechanism was the opposite one. Three fixes, each aimed at the measured failure: a window far longer than production (2s vs 500ms) so headroom is orders of magnitude rather than 2×; the premise **measured and skipped on** (`if burst >= debounce { t.Skip }`) so a machine too slow to emit a burst reports its own limitation instead of a product defect; and the message **polled for, not slept for**, so delivery latency cannot decide the outcome. The grace after the first message must be a FULL window — a split's second timer fires one window after the last write, so a shorter wait stops looking before the evidence arrives. Control the mechanism deterministically (100ms window, 150ms gaps → count 5) rather than trying to reproduce load, and verify the skip path actually fires (temporarily set the window to 1ns). This is the checklist item "tests don't rely on `time.Sleep` for synchronization" — the original even named the hazard in a comment without removing it. |
| CodeQL `go/incorrect-integer-conversion` (high) on `strconv.ParseUint(…, 16, 32)` narrowed to `int` | The parse width was chosen from the *field's* width in the file, not the *type's*. A TCP port is 16 bits and the kernel writes it `%04X`, so a 32-bit parse accepts values the caller then compares as if they were ports; where `int` is 32 bits the conversion wraps (`FFFFFFFF` → `-1`, `ok=true`) | `cmd/mxcli/docker/portowner_linux.go` (`hexPort`) | **Parse at the target type's real width and let the parser do the range check** — that is the whole fix, and it turns an unchecked narrowing into a rejection at the boundary. Establish reachability before rating it: the input here is `/proc/net/tcp`, written by the kernel, so no hostile value reaches it and the consequence of the wrap is a *missed* port match (the diagnostic falls back to its generic message), not memory unsafety. Two things make it worth fixing anyway — a range check that lives in the parser cannot be forgotten by the next caller, and the alert otherwise stays open forever. Measure the wrap rather than asserting it: a `GOARCH=386` binary **runs on an amd64 host**, so the 32-bit behaviour is directly observable, and the same run showed the repo does not currently build for 386 at all (`mdl/settingsoverlay` has `9007199254740992` as an untyped int constant) — worth knowing before claiming a 32-bit impact. A test written at 64 bits still catches it: at width 32 `hexPort` returns `4294967295, true` where it should refuse. Keep a 32-bit-safe test literal (`int(^uint32(0))`, not `4294967295`, which is not a valid `int` constant on 386). |
| CodeQL `go/unsafe-unzip-symlink` on a tar extractor that already checks the joined path and the symlink target — looks like a false positive | It is not. A **chain of two symlinks** escapes: the guard resolves each link against its **lexical** parent while the OS resolves it against its **real** one. `sub/up -> ..` genuinely is the root (allowed, correctly); `sub/up/w -> ..` therefore really is `root/w`, pointing at the root's **parent**, and lexically looks like `root/sub`. Then `sub/up/w/pwned` contains no `..` and passes every check | `cmd/mxcli/docker/download.go` — one `extractTarGzInto` on `*os.Root` behind both `extractTarGz` and `extractTarGzStrip1`, plus `tarEntryPath` / `symlinkStaysInside` / `pathWithin` | **Try to break it before rating it, and keep trying after the first six attempts fail.** Six single-step archives (absolute link, `../..` link, absolute name, link-to-root, …) were all correctly refused, which is exactly what makes "false positive" tempting; the seventh — two chained up-links — wrote a file into the extraction root's parent, and an eighth reached any sibling directory. The fix is `os.OpenRoot` + `Root.OpenFile`/`MkdirAll`/`Symlink` (Go 1.24/1.25), which hands containment to the kernel (`openat2` `RESOLVE_BENEATH`) instead of to string comparison — the failure is then `path escapes from parent` from the OS. Keep a **link-target** check as well and resolve its parent with `EvalSymlinks`: `os.Root` stops *mxcli* following an outward link, not mxbuild or the JVM that read the tree afterwards. Two things the rewrite fixed for free: `strings.Contains(name, "..")` silently dropped legitimate files (`foo..bar` never appeared, no error) — `filepath.IsLocal` is the right test, on path *elements* — and a `HasPrefix` containment test with no separator puts `/cache/runtime-evil` inside `/cache/runtime`. Settle "would refusing break real downloads?" by measurement, not caution: the 11.13.0 CDN tarballs are 3,646+279 (runtime) and 33,188+5,036 (mxbuild) entries with **zero symlinks**, listed with `curl \| tar -tzv` without saving the archive. Control both directions — the ordinary-archive test must pass, and against the old extractor the chained cases must actually write outside (they do, in both the stripping and non-stripping variants). |
| `mxcli check --references` refuses a page mxbuild builds, with "microflow data source M.F has no argument for parameter 'P' … does not fill it in, even when an object of the right type is in scope" (CE1571) | `mdl/executor/validate_datasource_args.go` | The rule was generalised from a sound measurement to a false one. A page **parameter** of the parameter's type does not auto-map (measured, still true); an enclosing **data context** of a compatible type **does**. The two are different things and the message asserted the wrong one as fact. Re-measured on mxbuild 11.13.0, five widgets in one `mx check`: nested in a dataview of the parameter's type → **no error**; matching context two levels up with a mismatched dataview between → **no error**; mismatched context → CE1571; no context → CE1571; page parameter of the exact type → CE1571. The walk now carries a `dataContext` (the entity types of the enclosing data containers), resolved from the container's data source — a flow's **return** type, a `database` source's entity, a `parameter` source's page-parameter type. An **association** or **selection** source marks the context *unresolved*, which **suppresses** the report: guessing wrong in that direction is exactly what rejected the working page. A **primitive** parameter is always reported (a data context can never supply a String), which is what keeps the rule sharp. The three rejected shapes are the controls — without them the fix is indistinguishable from deleting the rule. Generalisation is delegated to `entityCompatibility`, which accepts a relation in **either** direction: a missed CE1571 costs a build error mxbuild still catches, a wrong refusal costs a working page. |
| `mxcli check` warns MDL071 "attribute 'Year' is an OQL reserved word — … a view entity referencing it unquoted fails to build with CE0174" on a **non-persistent** entity | `mdl/executor/validate_oql_reserved_names.go`, `mdl/executor/cmd_enumerations.go` | The warning's premise cannot arise: an NPE has no table. Measured rather than reasoned about, by pointing a view entity at one — mxbuild 11.13.0 refuses the **reference**, not the name: `CE0174 "Entity 'X' cannot be used in OQL, because it is a non-persistable entity"`. `oqlUnreachable` skips a **known** non-persistent entity, for both the attribute name and the entity's own name. Persistence had to become **three-valued** (`entityPersistence`): `ALTER ENTITY … ADD ATTRIBUTE` carries no kind, and the two rules keyed on it want opposite defaults for "unknown" — MDL020 stays silent unless known persistent, MDL071 stays loud unless known non-persistent. The old boolean passed `false` for ALTER meaning *unknown*, so a naive gate on it would have silently dropped MDL071 from the path where a name lands on an entity that already has references. VIEW and EXTERNAL entities count as reachable — a view entity's own attribute name **is** its select alias, the one MDL071 case that genuinely needs a rename. |
| `mxcli check … --references` reports "nanoflow not found: Mod.Flow" for a nanoflow created **earlier in the same script**, printed directly under the line "(Note: References to objects created within the script are skipped)". `exec` runs the same file without complaint and `mx check` is 0 errors | `mdl/executor/helpers.go` (`validateWidgetReferences`) | One omission in a list of five. The function consults `sc.<kind>` — the same-script exemption — for microflows, pages, snippets and entities, and for **nanoflows alone** it did not, so every widget reference kind was exempt except that one. Fix is `&& !sc.nanoflows[ref]`, matching its four siblings. Note this is the **inverse** of MDL-ORDER01, which exists to catch a reference to something created *later*; a rule pair like that is worth checking in both directions when one half is added. The test asserts all the kinds in one table so the omission cannot reappear on a different line, and the control is a nanoflow in neither the project nor the script, which must still be reported. Reported as ledger #138; example `mdl-examples/bug-tests/ledger-138-snippet-nanoflow-same-script.mdl` |
| `create or modify translations in <Module> for <lang>` reports success ("Set 212 nl_NL translation(s) across 20 document(s)") and the app's pages switch language while the **menu does not** | `mdl/translations/outofscope.go` (new), `mdl/executor/cmd_translations.go`, `cmd/mxcli/syntax/features_misc.go` | The **navigation is a project-level document**, not a module one, so `in <Module>` never reaches it. Measured on the reporting project: 151 strings scoped against 546 unscoped, and re-running the same file unscoped landed 65 more across 22 further documents. Nothing warned — the document count was the only tell, and only if you knew what number to expect. A scoped run now names **the file's own entries** it did not reach (`translations.OutOfScope`), not "the project has other strings", which is true of every scoped run and would warn forever — the per-module workflow is exactly what the scoping exists to support. Second, load-bearing half: those entries were previously swept into the **drift** warning, whose premise ("no text has this as its source") is *false* about them — they matched, out of scope. They are subtracted from it, so "the text may have been deleted" is only said where it is true. Controls: an unscoped run of the same file reports nothing new and lands the strings; a key matching nothing anywhere is still reported as drift. Reported as ledger #137 |
| `mxcli run --local`/`--hub` sits at several hundred percent CPU for hours while the app is gone; `ps -o stat` shows the runtime JVM as `Z` (zombie) under it, `curl localhost:<app-port>` returns `000`, and the hub preview URL still answers | `cmd/mxcli/docker/localboot.go` (`watchExit`, `alive`, `stopProcess`), `cmd/mxcli/docker/runlocal.go` (`waitForInterruptOrExit`, `runtimeStoppedError`) | Two mechanisms. (1) **Nothing ever called `Wait()`** on the runtime process, so an exited JVM stayed an unreaped zombie — and `alive()` asked `Signal(0)`, which **succeeds on a zombie**. Measured (Linux 6.18, go1.26): proc state `Z`, `Signal(0)` → nil; after `Wait()` → "process already finished". So the liveness check reported a runtime that had terminated itself hours earlier as alive. `Signal(0)` is only a correct liveness test *because* something reaps — removing `watchExit` silently breaks that line, which is why the control is on the reaper, not on `alive()`. (2) **After boot, `run` waited on a signal and nothing else**, so a correct answer had no one asking; it now waits on the signal OR `rt.Exited()` and returns a **non-zero** error, because returning 0 after the app has gone is what let a supervisor conclude all was well. **Why it happens at all**: the local standalone runtime uses a development licence with a maximum run time and terminates *itself* (measured lifetimes 3h52m and 5h07m — not a fixed number, and shorter than a working session); `runtimeExitReason` lifts that from the runtime's own log, and reports nothing rather than guessing when it cannot tell. **Two waiters on one process deadlock**, so `stopProcess` consults the reaper's channel instead of taking its own `Wait`. The CPU spin itself was NOT reproduced and is not claimed fixed by name — it lived in the tunnel client, under a supervisor blind to its dead child; what is fixed is the state it occurred in, since mxcli now exits and takes the tunnel with it. **Generalisable**: a 200 from a tunnelled URL is not evidence the app is alive — the tunnel outlives the runtime. Reported as mxcli-formula1 FINDINGS §60 |
